figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: (Overview.) Structured SSMs independently map each channel (e.g. $D=5$) of an input $x$ to output $y$ through a higher dimensional latent state $h$ (e.g. $N=4$). Prior SSMs avoid materializing this large effective state ($DN$, times batch size $B$ and sequence length $L$) through clever alternate computation paths requiring time-invariance: the $(\Delta,\bm{A},\bm{B},\bm{C})$ parameters are constant across time. Our selection mechanism adds back input-dependent dynamics, which also requires a careful hardware-aware algorithm to only materialize the expanded states in more efficient levels of the GPU memory hierarchy.
figures.headline: The selective SSM layer adds input-dependent dynamics and materializes expanded states only in faster GPU memory levels.
citing_sentences: Details of the fused kernel and recomputation are in Appendix D. The full Selective SSM layer and algorithm is illustrated in Figure 1.

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: (Left) The standard version of the Copying task involves constant spacing between input and output elements and is easily solved by time-invariant models such as linear recurrences and global convolutions. (Right Top) The Selective Copying task has random spacing in between inputs and requires time-varying models that can selectively remember or ignore inputs depending on their content. (Right Bottom) The Induction Heads task is an example of associative recall that requires retrieving an answer based on context, a key ability for LLMs.
figures.headline: Time-invariant models solve standard Copying but fail Selective Copying, where input spacing varies and content must guide memory.
citing_sentences: To understand this principle, we focus on two running examples of synthetic tasks (Figure 2).

From the convolutional view, it is known that global convolutions can solve the vanilla Copying task (Romero et al., 2021) because it only requires time-awareness, but that they have difficulty with the Selective Copying task because of lack of content-awareness (Figure 2).

As discussed in Section 3.1, LTI SSMs (linear recurrences and global convolutions) can easily solve this task by only keeping track of time instead of reasoning about the data; for example, by constructing a convolution kernel of exactly the right length (Figure 2).

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: (Architecture.) Our simplified block design combines the H3 block, which is the basis of most SSM architectures, with the ubiquitous MLP block of modern neural networks. Instead of interleaving these two blocks, we simply repeat the Mamba block homogenously. Compared to the H3 block, Mamba replaces the first multiplicative gate with an activation function. Compared to the MLP block, Mamba adds an SSM to the main branch. For $\sigma$ we use the SiLU / Swish activation (Hendrycks & Gimpel, 2016; Ramachandran et al., 2017).
figures.headline: The Mamba block merges the H3 block and the MLP block into one repeated unit with an SSM on the main branch.
citing_sentences: H3 (Dao et al., 2023) generalized this recurrence to use S4; it can be viewed as an architecture with an SSM sandwiched by two gated connections (Figure 3).
We simplify this architecture by combining these two components into one, which is stacked homogenously (Figure 3).
Table 2 investigates the effects of the architecture (block) and its inner SSM layer (Figure 3).

figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: (Selective Copying.) Accuracy for combinations of architectures and inner sequence layers.
figures.headline: Only the selective layer solves Selective Copying, while gated architectures only partially improve accuracy.

figures.label: Figure 5
figures.caption: (Induction Heads.) Models are trained on sequence length $2^{8}=256$, and tested on increasing sequence lengths of $2^{6}=64$ up to $2^{20}=1048576$. Full numbers in Table 3.
figures.headline: Mamba generalizes perfectly on Induction Heads to sequence length 1048576, while other methods stay within 2× training length.

figures.label: Figure 6
figures.caption: (Scaling Laws.) Models of size $\approx 125M$ to $\approx 1.3B$ parameters, trained on the Pile. Mamba scales better than all other attention-free models and is the first to match the performance of a very strong “Transformer++” recipe that has now become standard, particularly as the sequence length grows.
figures.headline: Mamba is the first attention-free model to match Transformer++ scaling, especially as sequence length grows.
citing_sentences: We also compare against other recent subquadratic architectures (Figure 6).
Figure 6 shows scaling laws under the standard Chinchilla (Hoffmann et al., 2022) protocol, on models from $\approx 125M$ to $\approx 1.3B$ parameters.

We perform a series of detailed ablations on components of our model, focusing on the setting of language modeling with size $\approx 350$M models at Chinchilla token counts (same setting as Figure 6).

figures.label: Figure 7
figures.caption: (DNA Scaling Laws.) Pretraining on the HG38 (human genome) dataset. (Left) Fixing short context length $2^{10}=1024$ and increasing size from $\approx 200K$ to $\approx 40M$ parameters, Mamba scales better than baselines. (Right) Fixing model size and increasing sequence lengths while keeping tokens/batch and total training tokens fixed. Unlike baselines, the selection mechanism of Mamba facilitates better performance with increasing context length.
figures.headline: On DNA pretraining, Mamba scales better with model size and improves with context length, unlike the baselines.
citing_sentences: In particular, we focus on two explorations of scaling laws across model size and sequence length (Figure 7), and a difficult downstream synthetic classification task requiring long context (Figure 9).
In this experiment, we investigate the scaling properties of genomics foundation models with various model backbones (Figure 7 Left).
Figure 7 (Left) shows that Mamba’s pretraining perplexity improves smoothly with model size, and that Mamba scales better than both HyenaDNA and Transformer++.

figures.label: Figure 8
figures.caption: (Great Apes DNA Classification.) Accuracy after fine-tuning on sequences of length $2^{10}=1024$ up to $2^{20}=1048576$ using pretrained models of the same context length. Numerical results in Table 5.
figures.headline: Fine-tuned great apes DNA classification accuracy is shown for pretrained models at sequence lengths from 1024 to 1048576.

figures.label: Figure 9
figures.caption: (Audio Pretraining.) Mamba improves performance over prior state-of-the-art (Sashimi) in autoregressive audio modeling, while improving up to minute-long context or million-length sequences (controlling for computation).
figures.headline: Mamba improves over the prior Sashimi model in autoregressive audio modeling up to million-length sequences, controlling for computation.

figures.label: Figure 10
figures.caption: (SC09) Automated metrics for unconditional generation on a challenging dataset of fixed-length speech clips. (Top to Bottom) Autoregressive baselines, non-autoregressive baselines, Mamba, and dataset metrics.
figures.headline: Automated metrics on SC09 speech generation compare Mamba with autoregressive and non-autoregressive baselines.

figures.label: Figure 11
figures.caption: (SC09 Model Ablations) Models with 6M parameters. In SaShiMi’s U-Net backbone, there are 8 center blocks operating on sequence length $1000$, sandwiched on each side by 8 outer blocks on sequence length $4000$, sandwiched by 8 outer blocks on sequence length $16000$ (40 blocks total). The architecture of the 8 center blocks are ablated independently of the rest. Note that Transformers (MHA+MLP) were not tested in the more important outer blocks because of efficiency constraints.
figures.headline: SC09 ablations at 6M parameters vary center blocks of a SaShiMi U-Net while keeping outer blocks fixed.

figures.label: Figure 12
figures.caption: (Efficiency Benchmarks.) (Left) Training: our efficient scan is $40\times$ faster than a standard implementation. (Right) Inference: as a recurrent model, Mamba can achieve $5\times$ higher throughput than Transformers.
figures.headline: The fused scan runs 40× faster than a standard implementation, and Mamba reaches 5× higher inference throughput than Transformers.
citing_sentences: We benchmark the speed of the SSM scan operation (state expansion $N=16$), as well as the end-to-end inference throughput of Mamba, in Figure 12.

figures.label: Figure 13
figures.caption: (Ablations: Selective parameters.) $\Delta$ is the most important parameter (Theorem 1), but using multiple selective parameters together synergizes.
figures.headline: Making the step size selective matters most, and combining several selective parameters works better together.

figures.label: Figure 14
figures.caption: (Ablations: Parameterization of $\bm{A}$.) The more standard initializations based on S4D-Lin (Gu et al., 2022a) perform worse than S4D-Real or a random initialization, when the SSM is selective.
figures.headline: With selective parameters, standard S4D-Lin initialization performs worse than S4D-Real or random initialization.

figures.label: Figure 15
figures.caption: (Ablations: Expressivity of $\Delta$.) The selection mechanism of $\Delta$ constructs it with a projection of the input. Projecting it even to dim. $1$ provides a large increase in performance; increasing it further provides further improvements at the cost of a modest increase in parameters. State size fixed to $N=16$.
figures.headline: Projecting the step size input to dimension 1 gives a large gain, and larger projections add modest further improvement.

figures.label: Figure 16
figures.caption: (Ablations: SSM state dimension.) (Top) Constant $\bm{B}$ and $\bm{C}$ (Bottom) Selective $\bm{B}$ and $\bm{C}$. Increasing the SSM state dimension $N$, which can be viewed as an expansion factor on the dimension of the recurrent state, can significantly improve performance for a negligible cost in parameters/FLOPs, but only when $\bm{B}$ and $\bm{C}$ are also selective. Size of $\Delta$ projection fixed to $64$.
figures.headline: Enlarging the state size helps only when the input and output projections are selective, at negligible parameter cost.

figures.caption: (Scaling laws: extra ablations.) (Left) Instead of (Right) Instead of
figures.headline: Extra scaling-law ablations compare variant block designs against the homogeneous Mamba architecture.
citing_sentences: Figure 17 (Right) shows these variants compared to the original (homogenous) Mamba architecture.

figures.label: Figure 18
figures.caption: (Audio Pretraining (YouTubeMix) Ablations.) As a uniformly-sampled “continuous” signal modality, audio waveforms actually benefit from LTI models which have matching inductive bias. (Left) Homogenous models (all blocks have the same parameterization) (Right) Only the center U-Net blocks are ablated; the outer blocks are Mamba-S4. Purple line is same as figure on left.
figures.headline: On audio waveforms, the switch to selection is not always beneficial, since time-invariant models suit this continuous signal.
citing_sentences: Figure 18 shows that the change from S4 $\to$ S6 (i.e. the selection mechanism) is not always beneficial.

abstract: Foundation models, now powering most of the exciting applications in deep learning, are almost universally based on the Transformer architecture and its core attention module. Many subquadratic-time architectures such as linear attention, gated convolution and recurrent models, and structured state space models (SSMs) have been developed to address Transformers’ computational inefficiency on long sequences, but they have not performed as well as attention on important modalities such as language. We identify that a key weakness of such models is their inability to perform content-based reasoning, and make several improvements. First, simply letting the SSM parameters be functions of the input addresses their weakness with discrete modalities, allowing the model to selectively propagate or forget information along the sequence length dimension depending on the current token. Second, even though this change prevents the use of efficient convolutions, we design a hardware-aware parallel algorithm in recurrent mode. We integrate these selective SSMs into a simplified end-to-end neural network architecture without attention or even MLP blocks (Mamba). Mamba enjoys fast inference (5$\times$ higher throughput than Transformers) and linear scaling in sequence length, and its performance improves on real data up to million-length sequences. As a general sequence model backbone, Mamba achieves state-of-the-art performance across several modalities such as language, audio, and genomics. On language modeling, our Mamba-3B model outperforms Transformers of the same size and matches Transformers twice its size, both in pretraining and downstream evaluation.

sections.body: Transformer attention scales quadratically with sequence length, and earlier subquadratic models have trailed attention on language. The paper adds a selection mechanism in which the SSM parameters are functions of the input, so the model can keep or drop information depending on the current token. A hardware-aware parallel scan keeps this practical, and the selective SSM layers are combined into a simplified Mamba block with no attention or MLP blocks. The stated results include 5× higher generation throughput than Transformers of similar size, linear scaling in sequence length, and a Mamba-3B model that outperforms Transformers of the same size and matches Transformers twice its size. Results on audio and genomics are also reported.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Transformers are costly on long sequences, and Mamba adds input-dependent state space dynamics that scale linearly and match Transformers on language.

sections.body: This section defines structured state space models with four parameters, Delta, A, B and C, which map an input sequence to an output through a latent state. The continuous parameters are discretized with a rule such as zero-order hold, and the model is then computed either as a linear recurrence or as a global convolution. Because the parameters are fixed across time steps, the model is linear time-invariant (LTI). The authors argue that this fixed dynamics is a core limitation, since LTI models cannot reason about content. The section also reviews related architectures, including linear attention, H3, Hyena, RetNet and RWKV. It notes that the total hidden state has dimension DN per input, which costs O(BLDN) time and memory.
sections.heading: State Space Models
sections.headline: Structured state space models are linear time-invariant, so their parameters stay fixed across time steps.

sections.body: The section motivates selection with the Selective Copying and Induction Heads tasks, where time-invariant models fail because the spacing of relevant inputs varies. The change makes the step size, B and C functions of the input, so the model becomes time-varying and loses its convolutional form. A hardware-aware algorithm fuses discretization with a parallel scan, keeps the expanded state in fast SRAM, and recomputes intermediate states in the backward pass. The authors report that the implementation is up to 3× faster on A100 GPUs and scales linearly in sequence length. The section also simplifies the architecture into one repeated block that combines the H3 and MLP designs.
sections.heading: Selective State Space Models
sections.headline: Selection lets SSM parameters depend on the input, which breaks convolution, so a hardware-aware scan computes the model efficiently.

sections.body: Experiments cover synthetic tasks, language modeling with scaling laws and zero-shot evaluation, DNA pretraining, audio pretraining with autoregressive speech generation, efficiency benchmarks, and ablations. On Selective Copying, the selective layer solves the task while gated architectures only partly improve. On Induction Heads, Mamba generalizes to sequence length 1048576, while other methods stay within 2× the training length. The zero-shot comparison is against open source models trained for up to 300B tokens. The efficiency results give a scan 40× faster than a standard implementation and 5× higher inference throughput than Transformers. Ablations indicate that the selective step size is the most important parameter.
sections.heading: Empirical Evaluation
sections.headline: Experiments show Mamba solves synthetic recall tasks and outperforms baselines on language, DNA and audio, with 5× higher throughput.

sections.body: The discussion describes a continuous-discrete tradeoff: selection overcomes weaknesses on text and DNA, but it can impede performance on data that LTI models excel on. Ablations on audio waveforms examine this tradeoff in more detail. The authors state that the empirical evaluation is limited to small model sizes, below strong open source LLMs such as Llama, and below RWKV and RetNet, which were evaluated at the 7B scale and beyond. They state that it remains to assess whether Mamba compares favorably at larger sizes, and that scaling SSMs may involve engineering challenges not discussed in the paper.
sections.heading: Discussion
sections.headline: Selective SSMs trade off on continuous data such as audio, and scaling beyond small sizes remains unassessed.

sections.body: The conclusion restates the contribution: a selection mechanism added to structured state space models gives context-dependent reasoning while scaling linearly in sequence length. Inside a simple attention-free architecture, Mamba is reported to match or exceed strong Transformer models across a diverse set of domains. The authors name genomics, audio, and video as emerging modalities that require long context. The conclusion adds no new experiments; its support comes from the empirical sections on synthetic tasks, language, DNA, and audio.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Mamba is a strong candidate for a general sequence backbone, with selection giving context-dependent reasoning at linear scaling in length.

sections.body: Appendix A compares the selection mechanism with gating, hypernetworks, and data-dependence, using a GLU example to argue that these terms are too broad to be precise. Appendix B gives related work on S4 variants, SSM architectures such as GSS, H3, RetNet and RWKV, and older RNNs such as QRNN and SRU. Later sections give the SC09 speech training settings, including a learning rate of 0.002 and 200000 training steps at batch size 16. They also give the efficiency benchmark setup on an A100 80GB PCIe GPU and a memory comparison for 125M models, where Mamba's footprint is described as comparable to a Transformer with FlashAttention-2.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix covers selection versus gating, related work, speech-generation training details, and efficiency benchmarks.
